newsitem.title: PERU: Peru police moves leads to Red Cross safety worries.
newsitem.headline: Peru police moves leads to Red Cross safety worries.

text.p: Peruvian police movements around the besieged Japanese ambassador's home where Marxist rebels are holding 73 hostages forced the Red Cross on Wednesday to reduce its visits to the compound for safety reasons.

"The security situation has obliged the Red Cross to limit for the moment its presence within the residence," Red Cross spokesman Cecilia Baux told Reuters. "However, we will continue covering the hostages' basic needs."

The rebels fired several warning shots into the air early on Wednesday, apparently in response to stone-throwing and unusual movements by police special forces units in front of the compound the day before.
However, police kept up their war of nerves with the heavily armed 15 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels holed-up inside the compound.
They sent a helicopter flying above the residence and moved in black armoured personnel carriers with heavy machineguns to within two blocks.

The white helicopter made two series of flyovers in the morning and afternoon. It swept low between buildings around the residence, before gaining height each of the roughly dozen times it flew directly over the compound.
The helicopter did not buzz the building, but the rebels would have seen a policemen perched at its open door holding a machinegun.
After the first flyover, two Russian-made Caspir armoured personnel carriers drove around the residence and parked nearby, one aiming its machinegun toward the compound.
The MRTA made no immediate response to the manoeuvres. Last week, when a police helicopter hovered high above the residence, they fired three bursts of gunfire into the air.
The rebels, who have booby-trapped and mined the compound against possible attack, have fired warning shots on several occasions since the siege began. No one has been injured.
In the 36 days since the MRTA gunmen stormed a cocktail party at the diplomatic mansion, taking hundreds hostage, the Red Cross has delivered everything from food and water to chess sets and guitars.
The Red Cross will now limit itself to delivering meals and cleaning materials. The restrictions, however, were not expected to affect the Red Cross' mediator role.

In a clear signal to the rebels that Tokyo and Lima were united on how to handle the crisis, Japan's Lower House of parliament passed a resolution denouncing the rebels for "conducting criminal acts against the international community."

"We confirm the basic principle of not giving in to terrorism and urge the government to work toward a peaceful resolution of the crisis with the top priority on the lives of the hostages," the resolution said.
President Alberto Fujimori also basked in the approval of Washington for his handling of the crisis.

Fujimori "has been admirable in the way he's handled this problem," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters on Tuesday, in remarks trumpeted by Lima's pro-government press on Wednesday.
The president met in Government Palace with members of the Japanese media, who said Fujimori reiterated the main rebel demand of freedom for some 400 jailed comrades was unacceptable.
The rebels say they are ready to talk, but there is no point if their main demand for the release of their comrades is not on the agenda.
The MRTA initially took about 500 hostages after storming the residence but have released most in what they called "goodwill gestures."

The remaining 73 include two Peruvian ministers, generals, security chiefs, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats and the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors as well as Fujimori's younger brother Pedro.
